A1-A2.headline: The Amazing World Of The Great Dinosaurs

pages.text:
For millions of years, dinosaurs ruled the land on Earth. They first lived in the Triassic age and grew for a very long time.

Most died out in a huge event, yet science shows that today's birds are living dinosaurs.
pages.caption: Dinosaur

evidence.articleCaption: Dinosaur

pages.text:
In 1842, Sir Richard Owen gave them the name dinosaur, which means terrible lizard. Early experts thought they were slow and cold.

New science changed that view. Today we know many were quick and very active animals.
pages.caption: Sir Richard Owen's coining of the word dinosaur, in the 1842 revised version of his talk at an 1841 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Dinosaur coining of the word in 1841.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Sir Richard Owen's coining of the word dinosaur, in the 1842 revised version of his talk at an 1841 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science.

pages.text:
Dinosaurs came in many wild shapes and sizes. Some walked on two legs, while others walked on four legs.

Many grew sharp horns, tall heads, or hard skin. Some even had soft feathers long before birds flew.
pages.caption: Bruhathkayosaurus, potentially the largest terrestrial animal to ever exist

evidence.articleCaption: Bruhathkayosaurus, potentially the largest terrestrial animal to ever exist

pages.text:
Our study of dinosaurs has grown a lot since the first bones were found in the 1800s. At first, people thought those giant bones came from old tales.

Careful work with stone bones later showed their real past.
pages.caption: Restoration of two Centrosaurus apertus engaged in intra-specific combat

evidence.articleCaption: Restoration of two Centrosaurus apertus engaged in intra-specific combat

pages.text:
In the late 1900s, a new wave of study changed how we see these great animals. Scientists studied their bones and how they lived.

They proved dinosaurs were fast, smart, and far more active than people once thought.

B1-B2.headline: Uncovering The Secrets Of The Ancient Dinosaur World

pages.text:
For millions of years, dinosaurs stood as the main land animals on Earth. They appeared in the Triassic period and spread widely until a mass extinction struck.

Science now shows that modern birds are living dinosaurs.
pages.caption: Dinosaur

evidence.articleCaption: Dinosaur

pages.text:
In 1842, Sir Richard Owen created the word dinosaur, meaning terrible lizard, to capture their huge scale. Early scientists pictured them as slow and cold-blooded.

Modern research overturned that view, showing active creatures.
pages.caption: Sir Richard Owen's coining of the word dinosaur, in the 1842 revised version of his talk at an 1841 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Dinosaur coining of the word in 1841.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Sir Richard Owen's coining of the word dinosaur, in the 1842 revised version of his talk at an 1841 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science.

pages.text:
Dinosaurs displayed remarkable variety in size and body shape. Many walked on two legs, others moved on four, and some switched between both.

They also evolved striking features such as horns, bony crests, armor, and feathers.
pages.caption: Bruhathkayosaurus, potentially the largest terrestrial animal to ever exist

evidence.articleCaption: Bruhathkayosaurus, potentially the largest terrestrial animal to ever exist

pages.text:
Dinosaur science has come a long way since the first fossils were named in the nineteenth century. Early viewers mistook huge bones for mythical giants.

Later fossil finds built a clear picture of their ancient world.
pages.caption: Restoration of two Centrosaurus apertus engaged in intra-specific combat

evidence.articleCaption: Restoration of two Centrosaurus apertus engaged in intra-specific combat

pages.text: During the late twentieth century, a wave of fresh discoveries proved dinosaurs were far more lively than once believed. By studying anatomy and habitats, scientists uncovered how they grew, hunted, and lived on as birds.

C1-C2.headline: Scientific Reinterpretation And The Evolutionary Legacy Of Dinosauria

pages.text:
Across the Mesozoic era, dinosaurs dominated terrestrial ecosystems from the Triassic until a catastrophic mass extinction.

Evolutionary biology now classifies modern birds as living avian dinosaurs.
pages.caption: Dinosaur

evidence.articleCaption: Dinosaur

pages.text: In 1842, Sir Richard Owen coined dinosaur—terrible lizard—evoking their monumental stature. Early naturalists imagined sluggish ectotherms, whereas modern paleobiology reveals dynamic organisms.
pages.caption: Sir Richard Owen's coining of the word dinosaur, in the 1842 revised version of his talk at an 1841 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Dinosaur coining of the word in 1841.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Sir Richard Owen's coining of the word dinosaur, in the 1842 revised version of his talk at an 1841 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science.

pages.text:
Dinosaurian morphology spanned extraordinary diversification across bipedal, quadrupedal, and shifting postures.

Lineages evolved elaborate cranial crests, defensive horns, armor, and plumage.
pages.caption: Bruhathkayosaurus, potentially the largest terrestrial animal to ever exist

evidence.articleCaption: Bruhathkayosaurus, potentially the largest terrestrial animal to ever exist

pages.text: Paleontological inquiry matured dramatically after nineteenth-century scholars identified early fossils. While earlier observers mistook immense bones for giants, systematic excavation established prehistoric chronology.
pages.caption: Restoration of two Centrosaurus apertus engaged in intra-specific combat

evidence.articleCaption: Restoration of two Centrosaurus apertus engaged in intra-specific combat

pages.text:
The late-twentieth-century dinosaur renaissance revolutionized paleobiology by establishing active physiologies and complex behaviors.

Anatomy and ecology now clarify how these lineages thrived and endured as birds.
